en: The Sūtra on the Intention of Reviling Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Regarding the "Intention of Reviling" spoken by the Buddha: even if all the insects and ants of the ten directions were to devour one another, [the insects and ants of the ten directions...]
"All beings likewise devour me—why do you not know shame?
All the insects and ants of the ten directions have been my wives, and I too have taken all the insects and ants of the ten directions as my wives—why can you not feel abashment?"
The cycle of birth and death has lasted for a vast, incalculable duration; one should cultivate the seeds of the Path and must not cultivate the seeds of the karma of animals.
There are five offenses in committing sexual misconduct:
first, the loss of wealth and property.
Second, falling into alarm and fear;
third, fearing government officials;
fourth, encountering enmity and calamity.
Fifth, when one's life comes to an end, one falls into the evil hells.

Humans obtain their bodies through form and food; as humans, they have nothing to fear, yet they only dread becoming animals, from which they may then enter the realms of hell-beings or hungry ghosts.
The practitioner of the Way shaves off his beard and hair, practices begging for food, and endures hunger and thirst;
he leaves home and renounces wealth and property;
he does not look about with improper eyes, guarding the six sense faculties.
One avoids evil causes and conditions because one desires to escape suffering.

Furthermore, a single thought can give rise to calamities lasting for a hundred kalpas; it is like sowing grain that yields a hundredfold or a thousandfold. Although the grain has no consciousness, it constantly produces a ten-thousandfold return.
If people possessed true knowledge, they would surely realize more than this!
When a person sits in meditation practicing the Way, if they see sea creatures or any other objects, these were all creatures or things from their previous lives in the water.

If one is a bird or beast, having been a bird or beast throughout successive lifetimes, yet now encounters the right conditions, one’s transgressions will simply continue to multiply; everything one perceives will become a cause for sin. One must awaken to this mindset, for in previous lives, one shared the same realm as those in hell.
Past offenses constitute decline; present offenses are transgressions that have not yet become calamities.
Evil has its parents:
ignorance is the evil father, and craving is the evil mother.
Goodness also has parents:
the Sūtra on the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment is the good father, and the Six Pāramitās are the good mother.
Furthermore, there are other parents:
The Buddha is the father, and the Dharma is the mother.
To follow the Buddha’s words and act according to the Dharma is to practice as a child toward one's parents.
When a person falls into hell, the ghosts wish to strike them with clubs.
The person then thought to himself:
"This ghost will surely be extinguished before long!
With such a thought, he was immediately liberated and reborn in the heavens.
There are six things that cause one to sink into the Dharma:
first, not serving the Buddha;
second, not serving the Dharma; [and so forth].
Third, not serving the community of monks who observe the precepts;
fourth, not serving wise people;
fifth, not extensively instructing others to practice with diligence on the Path.
Sixth, the wise person who engages in debate.
These six matters serve to increase the Dharma.
One should not commit evil within merit; it is better to perform merit even within the midst of evil.
If a person, while in the state of training, does not practice the Way or recite the sutras, this is committing evil within merit;
if a person encounters illness and emaciation, official persecution, water or fire disasters, or the loss of wealth and property yet remains free from anxiety, this is creating merit within evil.

One should not commit offenses within the midst of merit; for instance, while burning incense, scattering flowers, or riding in a carriage, to scold others, saying "take this" or "wait for that," constitutes committing an offense within the midst of merit.
There are nine grades of killing, and thus offenses vary in their gravity.
One would rather kill a thousand ants than kill a single fly.
Thus, as one ascends to the level of human beings, killing a large being incurs a correspondingly greater offense.
Building a hundred Buddhist temples is not as meritorious as saving one person's life.
Saving all the people of the ten directions is not as meritorious as guarding one’s mind for a single day.
When a person attains a virtuous intention, their merit is immeasurable.
Giving to those who are evil persons will later serve as a causal condition for associating with evil persons; this is what constitutes receiving affliction.
Giving to those who are virtuous persons is what constitutes merit following in succession.
Furthermore, one should not accept goods from an evil person, for if one encounters them later, it will result in affliction meeting affliction.
It is better to accept goods from a good person and give them to a good person; one should not accept goods from an evil person and give them to an evil person.
It is better to receive the goods of an evil person than those of a good person;
it is better to receive the goods of a good person than those of an evil person.
When one receives an evil intention, it should be severed; when one receives a good [intention], that too should be severed.
Those with evil intentions [are reborn as] hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts;
those with good intentions [are reborn among] devas or humans—all these must be severed.
There are five Māras that give rise to confusion in people's minds, preventing them from attaining the Way:
First, the celestial Māra;
second, the Māra of transgression;
third, the Māra of conditioned activity.
The fourth is the demon of affliction;
the fifth is the demon of death.
When a practitioner of the Way walks the path, they should be aware of these five demons.
There are five matters that the Buddhas of the ten directions cannot alter:
first, the forgetting of one's past lives;
second, the rebirth in a higher realm when one's life is due to end.
Third, life shall come to its end and perish;
fourth, life shall grow old;
fifth, life shall die.
There is no one who can obstruct this matter.
A person in life has four things:
first, having good plans that are followed by auspicious signs.
Second, there are those with evil intentions accompanied by evil signs;
third, there are those with good intentions accompanied by evil signs;
fourth, there are those with evil intentions accompanied by good signs.
Whatever a person thinks, the mind perishes, the body perishes, and the causal conditions of what is seen also perish.

As for those who undergo calamity or fortune as a result of their actions in future lives, it is like planting a fruit; once this year’s fruit has ripened and fallen to the ground, there will be fruit again the following year.
Sin is like a tree, and the conditions of the mind are like its fruit.

Of the good and evil deeds performed by people, there are four deities who know them: first, the Earth Deity knows them; [the second is the Deity of the Four Great Kings; the third is the Deity of Heaven; and the fourth is the Deity of the Thirty-three Heavens].
Second, the celestial deities know it;
third, bystanders know it;
fourth, one’s own mind knows it.
There are three causes and conditions for firmly establishing the Path: first, practice;
second, reception.
Third is retribution (*āpatti*).
To commit evil deeds is "action" (*saṃskāra*);
once they have arisen, this is "feeling" (*vedanā*).
Once one has received [the fruits of karma], it becomes a calamity.

There were five sons of butchers who, upon returning home at dusk, immediately thought of the Way; later, when their lives ended, they were reborn in the evil realms. During the evening, they were entertained with the five kinds of music until dawn, and then, at daybreak, they were subjected to the five kinds of poison.
There are two kinds of people who receive the Buddha’s words: namely, those who are wise and those who are deluded; these constitute the two types.
Three things cannot be seen, just as when one maintains the precepts, various evils cannot be seen.
When a practitioner of the Way has transmitted the scriptures and practices the Path, there are four ways to receive merit:
first, practicing the Path with single-minded devotion while abstaining from food and drink, thereby receiving the veneration of others;
second, being naturally poor and possessing nothing, thereby receiving the veneration of others.
Third, one who dwells in self-sufficiency must not accept the prostrations of others;
fourth, when a person practices the Way, they should take only as much food as is necessary for sustenance and must not accept more than that.
If human speech accords with the sutras and the Dharma, it should be accepted; one should not refuse to accept it. The same applies to hearing the sutras.
When preaching the sutras for others, even if it disturbs their minds, there is no fault.

Why is this? When the Buddha originally preached the sutras, he did not wish to disturb the minds of people. Although preaching the sutras might disturb the minds of people, it is like one who is about to die from eating poison; by following the instruction to take an antidote, one will no longer die. The Buddha’s sutras are like that antidote which stops the poison.
A practitioner of the Way has four qualities by which fire cannot burn and weapons cannot harm them:
first, they have not yet received their assignment from the Buddha;
second, they have attained extinction.
Third, attaining the four dhyānas;
fourth, abiding in the mind of the Path rather than in birth and death.

When the Buddha was in the world and visited a household, the host would close the door, wishing not to let others see the Buddha; in a future life, such a person’s two eyes will be blind. For this reason, the Buddhist scriptures desire to reveal [the truth].
Dīpaṃkara attained the divine eye and thus gained far-reaching vision as well as radiance;
by providing the wick, he obtained fine eye sockets;
by providing the sesame oil and ointment, he obtained excellent pupils.
By giving fire, one attains the realization of the Truths.
From these causes and conditions, one obtains good eyes and lamps, and in future lives, one obtains vessels of gold, silver, and precious jewels.
When people come to speak of evil matters that confuse and delude the human mind, this is Māra; one must remain awakened regarding what is done.
This is called a good person obtaining evil parents; this constitutes a transgression.
When a demonic person comes to revile one, there is merely a wind; the ears should avoid it, for this is an evil wind.
If one does not avoid it, one will instead be struck by the wind of the evil person.
From these five, one attains a seat; through these five practices, one falls into the evil realms.
When entering an assembly of people, there are four types of persons who should be led out:
first, one who speaks what is not the Dharma to disturb the minds of others—upon arrival, they should be led out.
Second, seeing that what is being said is wrong, one does not restrain them but drags them out;

third, seeing that what they are doing is improper, one does not instruct them but drags them out; fourth, when their questioning is contrary to the Dharma, one no longer converses with them but drags them out.
Regarding those gathered among the assembly of practitioners on the Path: there are four causes and conditions for being bitten by fleas, lice, insects, or ants.
First, it is because one must undergo punishment for the consequences of past lives.
Second, it is because Māra comes to destroy the person, desiring not to allow them to attain the Way.
Third, not seeking a pure place;
fourth, not having an impartial mind.
There are eight types of people who are not to be trusted:
First, those who are greedy;
second, those who are envious;
third, those who are full of anger and malice.
Fourth, frivolous people;
fifth, government officials;
sixth, those with divided loyalties.
Seventh, those who harbor enmity;
eighth, women, government officials, water, fire, snakes, vipers, and sharp blades—these must not be approached, for approaching them leads to death.
There are five types of people regarding the *Tṛṣṇā-sūtra*:
first, those who desire to let others know that they possess the sūtra, because of their great desire for self-aggrandizement and the pursuit of fame;
second, those who wish to maintain the practice until its end, yet do not understand it themselves.
Third, desiring to rely on the sūtras to receive the veneration of others;
fourth, desiring that all people receive the sūtras from oneself alone because one wishes to be their teacher;
fifth, seeking the sūtras with the desire to escape birth and death and attain the path of transcendence, [thinking] that the path of the sūtras may be bestowed upon them.
There are five classes of those who study the sutras:
first, those whose intention is to hear many sutras;
second, those who wish to perform much merit.
Third, the desire to understand the sutras;
fourth, the preaching of the sutras for others;
fifth, the desire to sever birth and death.
The five types of envy are:
first, as when people serve a teacher together, desiring that he love only oneself and not loving others as well; this is called envy regarding dwelling.
Second, thinking to oneself, "I am merely a human being, born alone into a family of low status"; this is called envy regarding birth.
Third, seeing others possess wealth and desiring to be equal to them is the envy of material possessions (*āmiṣa-īrṣyā*).
Fourth, when the Buddha has profound sūtras, desiring to obtain them for oneself alone and not wishing for others to obtain them is the envy of the teachings (*dharma-īrṣyā*).
Fifth, seeing others are handsome and thinking to oneself that one alone is inferior is the envy of physical form (*rūpa-īrṣyā*).
One who commits these five jealousies shall not attain the Way.
A practitioner of the Way must not fall into the five disputes:
first, disputing over the Buddha;
Second, contention regarding the Dharma;
third, contention regarding the Vinaya;
fourth, contention regarding the Sūtras.
Fifth, disputing with the worthy.
A practitioner of the Way should not dispute whether something exists or does not exist.
There are five stubborn errors:
First, the stubbornness of physical error;
second, the stubbornness of verbal error;
third, the stubbornness of deviant error.
Fourth is the persistence of delusion through greed;
fifth is the persistence of delusion through admonition.
There are seven kinds of lust:
First, seeing the color of garments;
second, hearing the sound of pearl ornaments;
third, hearing the voices of women.
Fourth, to have thoughts in one's mind about women;
fifth, to gaze at them with the eyes;
sixth, to dwell upon the rituals of a married couple.
Seventh, the mental intention to commit [the act].
These seven types of sexual misconduct prevent one from attaining the Way.
There are five causes and conditions by which people easily forget:
First, forgetting the body;
second, forgetting through excessive discursive thought;
third, attachment to craving.
Fourth is attachment to views;
fifth is one’s original past life, which refers to having troubled people in former worlds and frightening them by interrupting their speech.
"Weariness and forgetfulness" refers to the weariness of mental attention.

Drinking alcohol results in poison for one quarter, drinking water results in celestial fortune for one quarter; lying down results in death for one quarter, and speaking virtuous words results in heaven for one quarter; speaking evil matters results in hell for one quarter—namely, the four quarters of hell.
The king had a wife whose younger brother was destined to enter hell.
The wife said to the king, "Do not let my younger brother enter this hell!
The king replied:
"Stop him for me. As her younger brother was about to enter, his wife said:
"This prison gate cannot be entered!"
The younger brother said,
"There is much to be found therein," and then he ran back into the prison.
In this way, people are led astray by their transgressions.
Suppose a person takes another’s plow yoke for use without returning it to its owner, intending to give it back after he has finished plowing.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be so; you have already committed theft!
The man said, "I wish to make a golden yoke to compensate for it."
The Buddha said:
"One who steals does not understand.
It is only when a person upholds the precepts that they are filial and obedient, thereby repaying the kindness of their parents."

Why is this? By not killing living beings, one attains longevity; by not stealing, one becomes wealthy; by being chaste, orderly, and non-deceptive, one gains trust; by not drinking alcohol, one remains pure. When parents occasionally fall into these states, they become peaceful and secure.
When staying overnight for a fast at a Buddhist temple, one must not lie upon a śramaṇa’s corded bed, a stool, a table, or within the bedding; to do so constitutes a violation of the precepts.
When a person invites a practitioner, the practitioner should not inquire about the scriptures before having eaten;
if the practitioner explains them [before eating], it is a transgression.
Only when one has eaten as a monastic may one inquire about the scriptures and the Way.

If one does not uphold the precepts and does not practice the Way, dwelling within a Buddhist temple is no better than throwing oneself into a cauldron; for in the cauldron, one merely burns a single body.
Those who do not uphold the precepts and do not practice the Way, yet remain within Buddhist monasteries, have burned countless bodies [in vain].
A practitioner of the Way should likewise preach the sutras; when people come to inquire about the sutras, one must not refuse them.
When a person brings an offering to a practitioner of the Way, one should not inquire about the scriptures; one may do so only later.
Furthermore, while receiving an offering, one should not preach the scriptures; to do so constitutes an offense.
There are five circumstances under which a practitioner of the Way should not accept an invitation: [list follows].
First, if one requests A and A is not as good as B, one should not proceed;
second, if one requests B and B is not as good as requesting A, one should not proceed;
third, if one requests A and A says that for his sake one should request B, then B should not proceed.
Fourth, if I come from afar and am not invited immediately, but only invited later, one should not go;
fifth, if one’s enemy does not wish it, yet one dwells in the same village or lives in close proximity to them.
If one is sitting in the midst [of the assembly], one should not walk about.
Why? Because walking causes the mind to become drowsy and distracted.
There are three types of cessation:
first, the cessation of the course of birth and death;
second, the cessation of the mental activity of the path because the mind ceases its engagement with the causes and conditions of birth and death.
Furthermore, there are three causes and conditions for a person who is prone to sleepiness or delights in sleep:
first, eating too much;
second, drinking; [and third, indolence].
Third is sorrow.
Furthermore, there are three causes and conditions for it:
first, the body comes to rest;
Second, because one has left the state of lying down and received a renewed intention;
third, because of the persistence of the reception [of life].

When a person lies down and awakens, there is intention, consciousness, vitality, life-force, breathing, and respiration; during the day, there are generally thirty-six thousand five hundred breaths, which are all complete and equal.
There are eight practices for removing drowsiness:
first, eating light meals;
second, sitting meditation;
Third, standing;
fourth, walking meditation;
fifth, reciting the sutras.
Sixth, observing the stars;
seventh, washing the face;
eighth, contemplating the bones.
If one does not understand, one should contemplate various wholesome matters; once the mind has shifted, it will naturally return to its object.
Because one desires to attain the concentration of the path of merit, one attains mindfulness of other matters and thereby achieves self-liberation.
There is merit gained through the body, merit gained through speech and mind, and merit gained through emptiness;
likewise, there is demerit incurred through the body, demerit incurred through speech and mind, and demerit incurred through emptiness.
"Empty acquisition of merit" refers to dreaming of obtaining gold, silver, rare treasures, nobility, wealth, or pleasure; this is called empty acquisition of merit.
"Empty acquisition of demerit" refers to dreaming that someone comes to kill one, or to invade one; this is called empty acquisition of demerit.

If one teaches others with one's mouth to commit evil, such as by encouraging them to kill, and later, due to those causes and conditions, is unjustly beaten by others, this is considered a transgression of the mouth;
if one commits the cause oneself and, through those conditions, is wounded or killed by another, this is considered a transgression of the mind.

The reason people have dreams of good or evil is that when they desire food and drink but have no actual objects, there is merely the mental intention; consequently, they dream of fine food and drink.
If the mind intends to kill someone, one consequently dreams of being killed by that person.
All things have causes and conditions, whether in past lives, future lives, or the present life.
A dream experienced during the first watch of the night concerns events of the morning or evening in the present.
Whatever good or evil is done in a dream is created by the mind; that which is encountered therein is likewise the mind.
For example, suppose a person takes up an object, examines it, and then puts it away.
Although it is no longer seen, the mental image of it arises immediately, no different from actually seeing it.
What was done in a previous life immediately confronts the mind of this present life.
As for those who, after death, remain seated or dwelling [in the intermediate state], they do so because during their lifetime they delighted in appearing as ghosts to terrify people;
or, when someone in the world falls ill, they speak to those nearby, calling out, "Wake me up!"
For this reason, having already died, they rise again and remain seated.
There are four causes and conditions for falling into the realm of the nāgas:
first, giving much in alms.
Second, being prone to anger;
third, treating others with contempt;
fourth, sitting with self-important arrogance.
These are the four matters that cause one to become a dragon:
the first results in the attainment of merit, while the latter three result in the acquisition of a dragon’s body.
As stated in the *Vinaya-sūtra*:

Among the various animals that have horns, it was because in previous lives they delighted in wearing horns, crossing them askew as a mark of beauty; thus they incurred the retribution for possessing horns and received the body of an animal.
As for those with unusual colors, it was because they were attached to colorful garments and, harboring evil intentions, greedily regarded them as beautiful; therefore they incurred this retribution.
Among parrots, there are those with red lips and beaks and red feet; these were, in their previous lives, fond of colorful robes and vermilion lips.
Women who delighted in wearing long skirts will, in future lives, fall among pheasants and peacocks with long tails; all of this is obtained now because of what was cherished in past lives.

If humans or animals have many sores on their bodies, it is because in a previous life they pierced the mouths of living fish or animals with wood or bamboo; thus they receive such retribution in the present life.

If people or animals see one another, some feel joy while others feel anger; this is because they were on good terms with one another in a previous life, so upon meeting in this life they feel joy, whereas if they were not on good terms in a previous life, they do not feel joy upon meeting in this life.
To be born as an animal is a result of evil merit; to feel joy upon obtaining food is what is meant by "evil joy.
This means that because such a person felt joy after committing evil in a previous life, they have obtained this retribution.
There are three causes and conditions why animals do not obtain fine food:
first, they have not practiced [virtue];
second, their wholesome merit is exhausted.
Third, their transgressions are natural.
Animals also desire forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile sensations, and they also communicate with one another, though they cannot speak as humans do.
As for women who have whiskers, they have come from among sheep, chickens, or ducks in previous lives; it is for this reason they have whiskers.
As for fish and turtles that have no voice, it is because in previous lives they severed the heads of those who were speaking.
Fish eggs do not hatch immediately; rather, they hatch after seven days.
If they remain on grass or wood in a dry place for forty or fifty years, they will only hatch upon encountering water.
As for why there are so many offspring, it is because those who commit evil deeds are numerous, and their karmic retribution arises simultaneously.
Those who are prone to anger, envy, delusion, and lust, and who practice these four, fall among the monkeys;
those whose actions are unstable and lacking in discernment likewise fall among the monkeys.
If a person delights in performing as a singer or acrobat, they will fall among birds, insects, or monkeys in future lives.
If they take pleasure in learning the art of killing for sacrificial offerings, they will fall among sheep in future lives. Why is this?
They sever people's scalps, flay their skin, and dismember them.
This is because in previous lives they delighted in kidnapping people and stripping them of their clothes and bedding, thereby incurring this calamity.
These insects likewise, in previous lives, kidnapped people and stripped them of their clothes and bedding, leaving them freezing cold as they huddled toward fires.
Therefore, one first incurs this calamity oneself: like a silkworm that freezes itself by its own silk, one dies within boiling water or fire.
The foolish who delight in killing become pigs in future lives;
those who terrify others become deer in future lives.
Those who were excessively greedy for fine flavors will become flies in their future lives;
those who delighted in beating others will become donkeys.
As for why they have long ears, it is because they enjoyed pulling at the ears of others.
Beasts love to seize people by the ear; some were perhaps soldiers in their previous lives. Why is this?
When one soldier shouts, the other soldiers all raise their voices in response.
When one donkey brays, the other donkeys also bray.
If one does not repay their debts, they will become an ox.
There are two causes and conditions for why an ox breaks its hooves:
First, being in debt;
second, being fond of wearing wooden clogs as a mark of refinement.
There are two causes and conditions for why a horse's hooves remain intact:
First, those who were in debt;
second, those who took pleasure in wearing wooden clogs as a mark of fashion.
There were six men who were companions, all of whom fell together into hell and were placed in a single cauldron, each wishing to recount his original transgression:
One person said, "Sa"; two people said, "Na"; three people said:
Regarding "chi" (持), four people said "she" (涉);
five people said "gu" (姑); six people said—
"Da-ra. When the Buddha saw this, he smiled. Maudgalyāyana asked the Buddha why he was smiling.
The Buddha said:

"There were six persons who were companions, together in a cauldron in hell; each wished to speak for himself as they leaped about in the boiling water, but they were unable to speak more than once, for as soon as each had spoken a single word, they sank back down."
The first person said, "As for 'sha' (沙), six thousand *koṭis* of years in the world constitutes a single day in hell; when will it ever end?
The second person said, "As for 'na' (那), there is no fixed term, nor do we know when we shall be liberated."

The third person says: "As for those who hold [possessions], alas! They should instead cultivate their lives through the means of livelihood; yet, being thus unable to restrain their own minds, they do not know contentment regarding the quantity of what they possess in this world."

The fourth person said, "As for 'the one who has fallen into calamity,' I have conducted my livelihood with utmost sincerity, yet it has caused my property to fall into the hands of others; thus, I am suffering pain.

The fifth person said, "As for 'the elder sister,' who can guarantee that I shall emerge from hell and no longer violate the prohibitions of the Path, thereby attaining rebirth in heaven and receiving the joys of the world?"

The sixth person says: "Dhara" means that this matter was not originally intended by the mind; it is like driving a chariot that leaves the main road, enters a wrong path, and breaks the spokes of the wheels—then regret is of no further avail.

The Buddha spoke of four barriers: from the world up to the sixth heaven is the barrier of death; from the seventh heaven up to the eighteenth heaven is the barrier of emptiness; from the nineteenth heaven up to the twenty-third heaven is the barrier of impermanence; and from the twenty-fifth heaven up to the twenty-eighth heaven is the barrier of transcendence.
To emerge from these four gates is the essential way of liberation.
The utmost limit of merit does not exceed the twenty-eighth heaven, and the utmost limit of evil does not exceed the Avīci hell; all other calamities and offenses vary in their degree.
From a single phenomenon arise the three poisons; from the three poisons arise the three evil realms.
Were there no three evil realms, all people would likewise attain the Way.
From the great Avīci hell up to the sixth heaven, they constitute a single realm.
From the seventh heaven up to the nineteenth heaven, they practice the four immeasurable minds together, forming yet another realm;
from the twenty-fifth heaven, they practice the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, extending upward to the twenty-eighth heaven, forming yet another realm.

Not liberated from the twenty-eight heavens and with the three poisons not yet exhausted, one descends again to become a human being, coming and going through the three realms; if one seeks the essential means of deliverance, one must extinguish discursive thought.
From the Avīci Mahāniraya up to the sixth heaven constitutes the realm of desire (kāmadhātu);
from the seventh heaven up to the nineteenth heaven constitutes the realm of form (rūpadhātu);
from the twenty-fifth heaven up to the twenty-eighth heaven constitutes the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), which is without thought, yet possesses thought.
From the Avīci Hell upwards to the twenty-eighth heaven constitutes the realm of birth and death;
beyond the twenty-eighth heaven is the unconditioned realm.
By severing lustful desire, one reaches the realm of form.
By severing ill-will, one falls into the realm of non-perception;
by severing delusion, one reaches the essential departure.
Within the three realms, there are three locations:
First, from the Avīci Hell up to the Sixth Heaven, these constitute the realm of lustful desire;
second, from the Seventh Heaven up to the Nineteenth Heaven, this is called the realm of attachment to form;

third, excluding the Four Heavens up to the Anāgāmin stage, and from the Twenty-fifth Heaven up to the Twenty-eighth Heaven, where there is neither perception nor non-perception, this is called the realm of formlessness.
These are the three bases: falling into birth and death, the revolving of formations, and attachment to form.
It is like the light of a fire which can only be seen but cannot be grasped.
Being in the state of sensual desire, being in the state of delighting in form—these are the three bases.
From the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, one should turn away from craving and lust for form and aspire toward the three realms of existence.
What is the essential path? There are three roots: [non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion].
There is the root of evil, the root of goodness, and the root of the Path.
Hell, animals, and hungry ghosts constitute the root of evil;
from among human beings up to the sixth heaven constitutes the root of goodness.
From the seventh heaven upward, one emerges through the twelve gates; this is the foundation of the Way.
If one has reached the twenty-eighth heaven yet fails to attain liberation, there are three causes and conditions:
the first is greed.
Second, there is delusion;
third, there is volition.
Therefore, one cannot attain liberation.
Having emerged from the twelve gates, one should wish for the absence of conceptual thought.
As for those who do not transcend the three poisons and have not yet attained liberation, it is because they have not yet exhausted them.
Why is there the heaven of the twenty-eight heavens?
In his previous life, while still in the world of mortals, because he was not greedy for his body and had a detached mind, he severed the seven external matters;
subsequently, upon receiving blessings in the sixth heaven, he severed the three internal matters.
Above the eighteen heavens, from the twenty-first heaven upward, there are four abodes belonging to the Anāgāmins.

Among those who practice the ten wholesome deeds, some are born in the first heaven above, while others are born in the sixth heaven above; because their cultivation of merit varies in degree, they do not reside in the same places.

Among those who commit the ten unwholesome deeds, some enter hell while others enter the realms of animals or hungry ghosts; because the gravity of their evil actions varies, they do not dwell in the same place.

Furthermore, one may perform wholesome deeds yet receive retribution for evil, or perform evil deeds yet receive retribution for good; within goodness there may be slight evil, and within evil there may be slight goodness, so subtle that it is imperceptible.
Within goodness there is no small evil, nor does one fall back into evil;
within evil there is no small goodness, nor can one escape from it.
The utmost evil does not exceed the Avīci Hell, and the utmost goodness does not exceed the twenty-eight heavens; because one fails to perceive subtle intentions, one cannot attain liberation.

All who practice the ten wholesome actions are born among gods and humans; as for why gods and humans are born by transformation (*upapāduka*), it is because when they were formerly in the world, they did not incline toward form and perceived the foulness of impurities, whereby they attained birth by transformation;
whereas those whose minds were inclined toward them would have entered the wombs of women.
There are five causes and conditions by which the various devas attain birth through transformation:
first, they do not associate with women;
second, no sensual thoughts arise in their minds.
Third, not desiring children;
fourth, delighting in sitting alone;
fifth, having no use for the world.
One who is not greedy for the body may also attain birth by transformation.
When a person's life is about to end, they should maintain their mindfulness; once they have finished reciting the breath, the mind will then be focused upon the inhalation and exhalation.
From the first heaven upward, this is the contemplation of the body through the calming of the mind, wherein one calculates that the body consists of thirty-two constituents:
hair, body hair, teeth, bones, skin, flesh, and the five viscera—these eleven things belong to earth;
tears, nasal mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, and urine—these seven things belong to water.
Warmth and heat, as well as digestion, these two matters belong to fire;
wind has twelve matters.
These thirty-two things all arise from earth, water, fire, and wind.
What is meant by "earth"?

Human birth arises from the vital essence of grain; the grain constitutes the earth, the mind constitutes the seed, and the vital essence constitutes the water. When these two unite, the body is produced.
Seeking a single garment and a single meal is for the purpose of nourishing the vital energy (*prāṇa*) and protecting the master’s body.
Because it is fundamentally non-existent, it is subject to extinction and impermanence.
Upon attaining the Way, one realizes that the body is not the self; one contemplates that the body will not endure long and must inevitably perish and decay.
When the mind takes on the nature of a human being, one must guard the mind with single-minded concentration.

A foolish person cannot protect their vital spirits (*po*, *hun*, and *shen*); they merely nourish the four limbs, deceived by the flavors of form, claiming "the body is the self. Calculating thus, they do not recognize evil; everything arises from the body through greed for food and taste, whereby they fall into suffering and wander through birth and death without liberation.

Originally encountering evil conditions, the soul and spirit depart in vain, following the paths of good or evil. When the body dies and falls to the ground, it decays and rots day and night; yet fundamentally, it was originally non-existent, existing only because of the activities of the mind that brought it into being. Once the body dies, it returns entirely to the earth; all things are likewise thus—having all passed away, they are impermanent.
People do not calculate for themselves, yet they harbor myriad thoughts, none of which are for their own sake; this is what constitutes suffering.

When the body dies and is cast aside, these myriad thoughts are likewise extinguished; this is what constitutes the self. Yet birth follows birth again in suffering, leading one to perform deeds of good and evil; the seeds sown remain unknown as to where they will lead—this is what constitutes that which is not the self.
When a practitioner of the Way practices the Way, they should act for the sake of severance.
If a person does not know the four types of impermanence, they will ultimately not attain the Way.

By personally reflecting on one's own body and observing all things subject to death and decay, one comes to know that persons and phenomena are all empty and that emptiness possesses nothing at all; when the mind thus remains stilled, one attains the practice of joy.
Once one has attained practice, the mind becomes peaceful.
Not being separated from these five [aggregates], the mind is unified; this is the Way.

When one examines the body for oneself and realizes there is nothing [substantial] therein, the mind abides in the body; likewise, regarding sensations, the mind, and phenomena, the mind also abides in them.
Cessation refers to three matters: the cessation of sensation (vedanā), and the cessation of the mental application regarding sensation. This refers to four matters:
the cessation of sensual desire and the cessation of the internal mental application;
the cessation of discursive thought (saṃjñā) and the cessation of volitional attention (manasikāra), which refer to the cessation of consciousness and the cessation of external phenomena.
These are the four foundations of mindfulness.
Having established them, one maintains them; having maintained them, one contemplates them.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Practicing both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* together leads to the attainment of the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Sitting alone and contemplating one's own mind means contemplating the cessation of form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)."

Regarding "mindfulness of the mind within": it is the cessation of the external mind through mindfulness; one constantly practices as it truly is, and perceives the Path as it truly is, because one sees for oneself while sitting and walking.
As the Sūtra says:
"A bhikṣu who can thus practice mindfulness of the mind within maintains that mindfulness."
One should first observe this mind, contemplating the cessation of thought; when mindfulness waits upon one's own mind, one then guards the mind.
When the mind does not depart from the body, it is for the practitioner to wait for the external, which refers to the myriad phenomena;
when mindfulness is within, it refers to contemplation.
One should cultivate the thought of the cessation of consciousness, constantly mindful that all things are impermanent and subject to decay; they are not mine, nor am I theirs.
When the urgent thought of death arises, what will you take with you as you depart?
"Maintain what is wholesome, maintain a single mind, and maintain the recitation of the sūtras, for these bring much joy.
The Buddha said:
"Take this which is yours; all else is not mine."

One should reflect with mindfulness that all meetings born of affection must inevitably end in separation; each person decays and perishes of their own accord. To dwell upon such things only disturbs the mind and increases one's transgressions. One must resolve to maintain purity within this body and proceed toward the path of Nirvana.
From the state of one-pointed mind up to the nine stages of decomposition, the Buddha contemplates that the four colors must all be extinguished.
He observes that when a person has been dead for four or five days, they begin to smell and decay, and their color turns a deep blue;
after five or six days, pus and blood emerge from the mouth, nose, ears, and eyes, appearing a vivid red.
Later, the muscles decay and rot, and worms arise within the intestines and stomach, which then eat their own flesh; the skin wastes away until the bones are exposed and stark white;
after a long time, they turn black and become like ash and dust.
Earth, water, fire, wind, and space are all not what I intend!

Since countless ages past, you have also been their wife or child, or their slave; you have also been livestock—oxen, horses, or insects—enduring toil and heavy debt, and being slaughtered, flayed, and roasted by others.

Now, when one takes others as one's wife, children, slaves, or servants, and likewise takes domestic animals such as oxen, horses, and insects, slaughtering, flaying, mincing, roasting, and hacking them at will, one shall surely undergo the consequences of these deeds once the body dies.
"O practitioner!

Have you ever seen a person who has died and their breath has ceased, such that they have no consciousness, their body is stiff and upright, and it becomes foul-smelling, ruined, and loathsome; when you contemplate this clearly, you become afraid and do not wish to see it?"
Why is there no fear?
Because it causes people to ascend to heaven and attain the path of Nirvana.
Since the Buddha knows that the nine realms are all empty and non-existent, he returns to abide in the single mind.

The practitioner of the Way must urgently extinguish discursive thoughts; when attending to things as they are without anything else, one immediately reaches the profound stability of phenomena. When practice is firmly established and both [subject and object] are present, that which is seen is not used because it does not abide, and thus it is not seen.
Volition, craving, and thoughts are impermanent and subject to decay; one should contemplate the antidote to lust, the antidote to anger, and the antidote to delusion.
Past actions are not constant; the unconditioned is peaceful and secure. Yet people do not know impermanence; they never cease their greed and do not depart from the realm of hungry ghosts (preta).
All that exists in the world is like a dream; one may see fine food in a dream, yet upon waking, it is no longer seen.
All things in the world are likewise: as soon as they are born, they die; as soon as they are formed, they decay. Since they must all ultimately return to emptiness, what is there to crave?
It is the same for people who have wives, children, and property. Why is this?
When a person engages in business and acquires wealth and profit, they rejoice if their family members are gathered together.
For example, it is like a gathering of flying birds; all are impermanent, and once they part ways, they are no longer seen.
Even if things were permanent, there would be myriad forms of sorrow and fear; dwelling within the cycle of birth and death, one accumulates sins day by day.
The wise person disciplines themselves to have few desires, seeking only one robe and one meal;
they follow the practice of meditative concentration, do not seek a fixed dwelling place, constantly return to guarding the purity of the body, sever the pursuit of gain, and contemplate emptiness.
Question:
"From what does the practice of the Way and the guarding of the mind originally arise?
He replied:
"The nature of heaven and earth is thus established; humans descend from the fifteenth heaven above, their lifespans free from untimely death.
One is uprooted from the five paths of birth and death, which arise from the six decays."

The mind and intentions of human life are inherently good; they are originally free from craving, sensation, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, yet they are deceived by the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.

The eyes first perceive forms; the ears hear sounds; the nose discerns fragrances; the mouth perceives flavors; and the mind forms thoughts. These ten activities constitute the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The intellect (*manas*) functions as consciousness (*vijñāna*); together they form the six bases of decay (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Through these, one plants the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, and from this, there arise for me old age, sickness, death, and birth.

Seeking the Way within the five realms of existence in order to sever birth and death, one maintains the cessation of mental activity: the eyes cease from forms, the ears from sounds, the nose from fragrances, the tongue from flavors, and the body from pleasant sensations; one abandons the six decaying activities, contemplates the destruction of mental conceptions, and sits in meditation to extinguish the mind.
One who realizes the Way extinguishes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Knowing that they are fundamentally non-existent, one contemplates emptiness and perceives emptiness, proceeding directly toward the gate of *nirvāṇa*.

For one who maintains this state, the mind becomes the master of consciousness; thus, the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are essential for the calamities [of rebirth], as their activity constitutes the root of the seeds for wandering through the five destinies.

The practitioner of the Way applies refined contemplation and maintains the fourfold intentionality; desiring to abide in non-evil, they reflect: "Where do mindfulness, cognition, and conceptualization run?
When a person wishes to extinguish mindfulness, cognition, and conceptualization, they should practice all-encompassing conduct rather than severing the ten matters of the body.
When the three matters of body, speech, and mind are concentrated, the five aggregates and the six sense-fields are then rectified.
As for the three concentrations:

when the mouth has no [discursive] knowledge, it is concentration of speech; when the body has no [discursive] knowledge, it is concentration of body; when the mind has no [discursive] thoughts, it is concentration of mind.
The mind has four ailments; that which is characterized by an abundance of delusion refers to an abundance of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
When the five aggregates abound, the mind wanders and cannot proceed rightly.
Being unable to proceed rightly, it gives rise to anger and lustful thoughts; being unable to restrain them, one falls back into delusion.

Therefore, practicing the Way requires that one must sever the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); severing the five aggregates means severing painful sensations, itching, unease, and excessive desire.
The Master said:
"The body does not wish to move because it is exhausted by excessive fatigue."
"It is because the mind does not wish to practice, nor does it wish to contemplate death, decay, suffering, or emptiness.
He asked: "What is meant by 'original birth'?"
The Master said:
"It means that non-doubt is the root from which it arises.
[He asked: "What is its direction?"
"What is the 'counterpart' (pratipakṣa),
and what is 'practice' (caryā)?
The Master said:
"Not turning the mind constitutes the direction; not turning the thought constitutes the confrontation; and being agreeable constitutes the practice.
He asked: "What kind of field is this?"
"Who is called the field?
[The Buddha replied: "You, sir, possess intention; the farmer does not know whether he has intention or not!
The farmer is unaware; you, sir, possess the awareness of intention, whereas the farmer lacks the awareness of intention!"
One may say that mental cognition is the mind;
the flavor of lust is also the mind. Why is this so?
"It is not that [the field] is near;
for one who has left the household life, there is no field. This is what it means.
Question:
"Is it that there is intention regarding the Buddha’s homeland, yet no intention [regarding other things]?

"It is so; fundamentally, there is neither body nor intention. One merely creates this and thereby obtains this. For example, among the five kinds of seeds, they do not arise without seeds; likewise, human birth is also fundamental, yet it occurs even though there is no seed."
It is like lighting a fire: when the flames emerge, they form embers;
once the embers have consumed the fuel, the fire ceases.
When a person realizes that the self is not a self, all phenomena likewise come to rest.
An objection was raised:
"If there is fundamentally no intention, for what purpose is one to maintain [this state]?
The Master said:
"Because that which is used is fundamentally non-existent, it can be maintained;
because that which is extinguished is fundamentally existent, it cannot be maintained.
The Master said:
“The Path has four essentials:
first, the multitude maintains the gate;

second, knowing that the body is not the self, one then destroys attachment to the body and no longer cherishes it; this is called for the person to exit through the gate and reach the gate of the sixth heaven.”

Third, knowing that all things are impermanent and no longer directing the mind toward them; this is called exiting the door of the eighteenth heaven. Fourth, like emptiness extinguishing emptiness; this is called exiting the door of the twenty-eighth heaven, for it is through the extinction of emptiness that one falls into the Path.
The Sūtra says:
"One who practices the Way and attains awakening achieves liberation; that is, awakening to suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impermanence.
To achieve liberation means to transcend the four essential realms and attain the seven heavens above the First Dhyāna, where there is only the body and its shadow.
Why is this? Because practicing the Way involves the decay of the body.

One contemplates the body by observing the head, hair, and brain; one contemplates that the hair originally has no place from which it comes, and though produced through conditioning, it must all eventually rot and fall away.
The brain is like congealed rice gruel and will all become putrid and foul;
the eyes have only hollows, from which watery fluids should flow out into the void;
the ears have only hollows, from which filth and water leak out.
The saliva and nasal mucus from the nose and mouth shall all flow out, being discarded, scattered, and dissolved;
the tongue, throat, lungs, liver, heart, and the foul blood within the heart;
the gallbladder, diaphragm, spleen adhering to the stomach, the kidneys adhering to the spinal vertebrae, and the flavors within the stomach that digest food; all these shall likewise perish.
The large intestine contains feces; the small intestine has orifices for urine and excrement, and the lesser intestines all become bloated and rot;
the intestines and stomach drench one another with feces and urine, becoming a loathsome stench;
below are the buttocks, blood, both shins, and both feet, where the flesh and muscles have completely wasted away and the tendons and veins have decayed.
The skeletal chain falls apart joint by joint;

the shins are straight, firm, and pure white, while the thigh bones are like chariot wheels. The pelvic bones are connected to the spine, and the shoulder blades are connected to the elbows, arms, and hands. The skin and leather also wither and rot, falling away joint by joint;
the neck bones are connected to the skull, and as the flesh and blood are entirely consumed, they turn back into ash and dust.
All wriggling creatures, when they cease to breathe out and thus pass away, their bodies become rigid and no longer move. When the fire element departs, the body grows cold;
when the wind element departs, the breath ceases; when the liquid element flows out from the nine orifices, it is the departure of water; and when they no longer eat, it is the departure of earth.

After three or four days, the color turns bluish-black; pus and blood flow from the mouth, nose, ears, and eyes, emerging from all nine orifices. The skin, bones, and flesh completely decay, and the intestines, stomach, five viscera, and limbs—all are reduced to ashes and dust.
Viewing all phenomena in this manner, one sees that one's own self is likewise so—all things are extinguished and become emptiness.
By clearly knowing that the out-breath and in-breath are also empty, one may draw near to the Way.
The Sūtra on the Intention of Reviling Spoken by the Buddha
